note: Verse 3 promises that those who reach the feet of the one who went upon the flower will live long 'above the earth' (நிலமிசை நீடுவாழ்வார்), which Parimelazhagar takes as the world of release. In 1103 a lover asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு) is as sweet as sleep on the soft shoulders of the one he loves (இனிதுகொல்). The conflict holds only if நிலமிசை is read with Parimelazhagar as a heavenly world and the lover's question is taken as a real ranking; on Manakkudavar's reading (long life on earth) the two do not meet.
reason: 1103 is a lover's rhetorical இனிதுகொல் about தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு; verse 3 promises நீடுவாழ்வார் to devotees and says nothing about sweetness or about that world. The conflict needs both Parimelazhagar's நிலமிசை as heaven and the lover's hyperbole taken as doctrine, and even then the claims do not address the same thing.

note: 683 sets two groups side by side: among spear-bearers (வேலாருள்) the envoy speaks of victory, and among treatise-knowers (நூலாருள்) he is master of the treatise. 727 pairs the same two things as a simile: the treatise learned by one who fears the assembly is a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி among enemies. In both the treatise is treated as the speaker's weapon, and 727 adds that it is useless without the nerve to use it.
reason: 683 only names two audiences, நூலாருள் and வேலாருள், with no simile; it does not treat the நூல் as a weapon. 727's image is a வாள் in a பேடி's hand. The shared 'image' is supplied by the note.

note: 709 says the eye itself declares enmity and friendship to those who can read it. 828 says a weapon is hidden even in an enemy's hands folded in worship, and the tears his eyes shed are the same (ஒன்னார் அழுதகண்ணீரும் அனைத்து). On the reading that the eye cannot conceal, which Parimelazhagar states under 710, the weeping eye of 828 should not be able to deceive; 828 holds that it does.
reason: 709 is conditional (கண்ணின் வகைமை உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்) and 828 warns that ஒன்னார் அழுத கண்ணீர் hides a weapon; it does not say the tears succeed in deceiving, and Parimelazhagar addresses 828 to those able to read signs, so the claims are compatible.

note: 739 says lands that give riches only when sought are not lands (நாடல்ல நாட வளந்தரு நாடு); Parimelazhagar takes நாடுதல் as searching with toil. 1031 says ploughing is foremost even though one toils at it (உழந்தும் உழவே தலை). On Parimelazhagar's reading, 739 counts the need for toil against a land while 1031 honours the toil that produces its yield; if நாட means only that the inhabitants need not go looking elsewhere, the conflict fades.
reason: 739 judges a land (நாட வளந்தரு நாடு நாடல்ல) and 1031 ranks an occupation; உழந்தும் itself concedes toil is a cost, so the verses do not make incompatible claims even on Parimelazhagar's reading of நாட.

note: 768 allows an army without strength to gain stature from its bearing. 273 says one without strength putting on the form of the strong (வலியில் நிலைமையான் வல்லுருவம்) is like a cow grazing in a tiger's skin. On Parimelazhagar's reading of படைத்தகை as outward show, 768 credits what 273 mocks; 273 is about a false ascetic, so the conflict holds only if both are taken as claims about appearance without substance.
reason: 768 concerns an army's repute from படைத்தகை and 273 a false ascetic's வல்லுருவம்; they do not speak of the same thing, and the note concedes the conflict exists only if both are abstracted into claims about appearance.

note: 778 says the lord's anger does not reduce the standing or ardour (சீர்) of fearless warriors. 895 says those who have drawn the anger of a king of fierce might (வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர்) will not survive anywhere they go. Both use the verb செறு for the king's anger; 778 marks a case where it is harmless, anger at excess of loyal zeal, while 895 concerns those who offend the powerful, whom Parimelazhagar takes to be rival kings.
reason: The link rests on the shared verb செறு. 778 says warriors' சீர் does not shrink even if இறைவன் செறினும் (Parimelazhagar: even if he forbids the fight); it does not say the king's anger is harmless, and 895 வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர் is about offending a mighty king. Neither limits the other.

note: 664 says saying is easy for anyone and doing as one has said is hard (சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்). 779 takes the hardest case, a sworn vow in battle, and says the one who dies in the attempt cannot be blamed for failing. Death in the effort is accepted as having kept one's word, a limit on how literally 664's standard is applied.
reason: 664 (சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல் அரிய) is an observation that carrying out a stated plan is hard, not a standard of blame, and it is not about vows; 779's இழைத்தது இகவாமைச் சாவார் cannot be a limit on a standard 664 never sets.

note: 790 distrusts the declaration of how close two friends are; Parimelazhagar says that speaking of 'they' and 'we' already introduces a separation. In 1209 a woman says her life is ending as she thinks of the unkindness of the man who used to say 'we are not separate' (வேறல்லம் என்பார்). Her complaint is a speaker's case of what 790 states in general: saying the closeness did not make it so.
reason: 790 says that describing the bond (இனையர் இவரெமக்கு ... என்று புனையினும்) makes friendship புல்லென்னும், a point about praise cheapening it; it does not say that declaring closeness fails to make it true, which is the claim the note needs to connect it with 1209's வேறல்லம் என்பார்.

note: In 1237 she asks her heart whether it will win any glory by telling the cruel one, as Pope renders it, of the uproar over her wasting shoulders (பாடு பெறுதியோ நெஞ்சே ... உரைத்து). In 1200 she tells the heart that reporting its pain to one who is not close is harder than filling the sea. Both are addresses to the heart that reject sending him word of her suffering.
reason: 1237's பாடு பெறுதியோ ... உரைத்து is read by both Parimelazhagar (சென்று ... சொல்லி மேம்பாடு எய்தவல்லையோ) and Manakkudavar (நீ அவர்பாற் போகல் வேண்டுமென்று) as urging the heart to go and tell him, so it does not reject sending word; only 1200's உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய் calls telling futile.
